He, then, was persuaded by his counsel,
and sent to Tzimiskes and promised to submit,
and to accept upon himself a tribute of three hundred thousand zuzes.
And he, King Tzimiskes, also agreed to this.
And when he drew near to Damascus,
Alptakin came out to meet him,
and dismounted and kissed the ground before him several times.
And the king was pleased with this,
and made him ride and honored him.
And he commanded that he recount before him and show his valor.
And when he recounted it,
the king praised him;
and again he got down and kissed the ground.
And he commanded, and made him ride;
and he remitted to him the tribute of one year;
and again he got down and kissed the ground.
And the king requested of him the horse upon which he had recounted {his deeds}, and his armor, and his spear.
And he presented these along with other vessels and gifts,
and twenty mares in addition, and a multitude of spears.
The king, however, accepted that horse alone and one spear alone;
and the rest he returned, and expressed his gratitude.
And he clothed Alptakin in royal garments,
and gave him jewelry and silver vessels and mules.
And he left and went to Sidon;
and its inhabitants came out to submit to him,
and brought him gifts.
And he left them and went against Beirut;
and with the sword he conquered it and plundered it.
And he went against Byblos (Jbeil);
they too showed themselves rebellious.
And he took it also with the sword and plundered it;
and he departed and went to Tarsus.
And there the brother of Queen Theophano gave him deadly poison to drink,
and he became severely ill.
And he set out for the capital city (Constantinople);
and there he died, after having reigned for four years.
This man was exceedingly energetic in his military service,
and strong in his body,
and brave in his soul,
and victorious in battles.
And when he reigned,
he showed magnanimity toward everyone,
and released the prisoners,
and built a great church in Constantinople,
and subjugated many cities and regions.
And the nobles and all the people mourned greatly over his death.
And after him, Basil and Constantine, the sons of King Romanos, reigned {OCR?} fifty-eight years;
and they were in true love with one another.
